appraisal_events.evidence: M. de Guermantes, presque à chaque nom qu'on prononçait, s'écriait : « Mais c'est un cousin d'Oriane ! » avec la même joie qu'un homme qui, perdu dans une forêt, lit... un enfantillage... réduisait sa grandeur nobiliaire à de simples supériorités domestiques
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator ironically likens M. de Guermantes' compulsive genealogical 'cousin d'Oriane' refrain to a lost traveler's naive relief at a small signpost, framing the aristocratic obsession with kinship as a charming but childish narrowness that reduces noble grandeur to petty domestic one-upmanship.

appraisal_events.evidence: les absurdes histoires touchant le charmant grand-duc héritier de Luxembourg trouvaient créance dans ce salon... On reprit les mêmes faux récits, on en ajouta d'autres; le nègre... 'grand-duc méchant, c'est épatant'
appraisal_events.explanation: A wave of hostile gossip and a servant's damning anecdote about the grand-duc spread and gain credence in the salon, but the narrator explicitly flags these stories as absurd and false, undercutting their reliability even as they locally damage his reputation.

status_effects.explanation: His repeated, unreflective genealogical enthusiasm is gently mocked by the narrator as childish and self-limiting, even as the narrator also finds it charming.
Gossip and a servant's complaint locally tarnish his reputation in the salon, even though the narrator signals the stories are unreliable.
Her attempt to defend her nephew is explicitly said to supply ammunition against him, so her intervention backfires and weakens her own advocacy.

ambiguities: 'Le général' who converses about genealogy with M. de Guermantes is inferred to be M. de Beauserfeuil, named later in the same passage, but this identification is not made explicit by the text.

The narrator explicitly calls the gossip about the grand-duc 'absurd' and made of 'false stories,' so although it gains credence within the salon, the passage does not endorse it as true; this tempers how negatively the grand-duc's local status should be read.
